cit.q: seeing that the post has been ruined in the noisy shed [for elephant bulls]...

note.p: A borrowing from Sanskrit śālā 'hall, house, shed' (NWS), denoting a shed or hall attached to a household. This is probably its earliest attestation, and the only one in first-millennium texts in which it denotes a stable. In all other occurrences it refers to a sugarcane press-house, i.e. the shed in which cane was crushed and its juice boiled down into sugar, the press itself being called entiram (from Skt. yantra). Given the isolated nature of this attestation, it is also possible that the outbuilding called ālai in question was in fact a 'press-house', but one large enough for an elephant to spend the night there, tied to a hitching post, during the cold season.

cit.q: entiram cilaikkum tuñcāk kampalai / vicayam aṭūum pukai cūḻ ālaitoṟum / karumpiṉ tīm cāṟu virumpiṉir micaimiṉ

You, who desired [it], enjoy the sweet juice of the sugarcane of all the press-houses surrounded by smoke, where the jaggery is being boiled, where the clamour does not cease, and where the machines resound!
the fire at the press-houses fragrant from dark sugarcanes
aṟai uṟṟ' / ālaikk' alamarum tīm kaḻaik karump'-ē
the sugarcane with sweet stalks, which whirl in the press-houses [for pressing] after being cut/being beaten (aṟai uṟṟu)
ālai-toṟum ñerēreṉak / kaḻai kaṇ uṭaikkum karumpiṉ ēttamum

the sounds of sugarcane that is rapidly crushed at [its] stalks in all the press-housesThe press-house is possibly compared to a rain cloud because it is dark (with smoke from the boiling), it roars (with the noise of crushing), and it is full of liquid (the sweet juice, like rain). that looked like rain clouds
"... along with the smoke from the press-houses of boiling and crushing"
Yacōtai with sweet speech like sugarcane for the press-house
O [you who are] like a long sugarcane for the press-house!
cit.ref: Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 7.1, line 1 (trans. by Erin McCann)

cit.q: Lord of lovely Āli scented by the smoke rising everywhere from the [sugarcane] press-houses
Nānkūr that is fragrant from the smoke of the [sugarcane] press-houses in the fields where [the juice] boils up

note.p: As demonstrated, the sugarcane context is well attested. This usage has close parallels with Sanskrit and Pali terms for sugarcane-processing sheds, such as īkṣuśālā and yantraśālā in the Avadānaśataka (tale 41) and ucchusālā in Buddhaghosa's Atthasālinī. Cf. entiram)
The mediaeval commentaries on 19: 23, 260–262 and Maturaikkāñci 258 gloss ālai as 'press'. This probably reflects a later shift from the building to the device it housed.

The word is also attested in an eleventh-century inscription on the walls of the Vīrattāṉēśvara shrine at Kīḻūr, near Tirukkōyilūr (South Indian Inscriptions, vol. 7, no. 863; p. 434 = A.R. No. 236 of 1902; digital edition: DHARMA, SII 7.863). Describing the surroundings, the text reads: veḷ pūm karump' iṭai tuṇittaratt' āṭṭ' oli ālai ayalatu 'in the vicinity of the shed [with] the grinding noise (āṭṭ' oli) [caused] by those who cut the white-flowered sugarcane in the middle.' Here, too, ālai denotes the building in which sugarcane was crushed, and the verb āṭṭu- 'to grind, crush' describes the process. For the same verb denoting the same process, cf. Nālaṭiyār 34.1: karump' āṭṭik kaṭṭi ciṟukālaik koṇṭār those who, having crushed the sugarcane, took the jaggery in good time/at dawn.

A thirteenth-century inscription of the Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam (South Indian Inscriptions, vol. 4, no. 511; pp. 147–148 = A.R. No. 64 of 1892; digital edition: DHARMA, SII 4.511) mentions the compound ālaikkarumpu that designates sugarcane grown specifically for crushing in the press-house, as distinct from other crops of the land.
